newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU farm ministers discuss beef crisis measures.
newsitem.headline: EU farm ministers discuss beef crisis measures.

text.p: European Union agriculture ministers on Tuesday discussed ways to compensate angry farmers for a beef price slump caused by the mad cow crisis that has isolated Britain from its partners.

Thousands of Irish farmers were converging on the ministers' rural conference hotel to give vent to frustration at a 40 per cent drop in incomes after Britain announced a link in March between mad cow disease and a fatal human illness.

Ministers were also expected to put pressure on British Agriculture Douglas Hogg to explain his government's suspension of part of a cattle cull supposed to eradicate the disease in Britain and restore shoppers' confidence in the meat.

They are refusing to lift a worldwide ban on British beef until the London government carries out in full a plan drawn up at an EU summit in Florence last June and are angry at what they see as an U-turn by Prime Minister John Major.
Irish Agriculture Minister Ivan Yates, whose country is current EU president, urged his colleagues to "look serious" at a group photograph they posed for hours before the formal talks closed.
"There are 8,000 farmers outside. We must look serious," he said in a lighthearted aside as ministers joked before the final session of talks in Killarney, southern Ireland.
The protest is timed to coincide with discussion of measures to restore confidence in beef and to compensate farmers for a sharp drop in household consumption of beef and in farmers' income.

"It'll be very noisy. It will be difficult to restrain them as they express their anger, concern and frustration with the Irish government and the EU," said Derrick Cunningham, spokesman for the Irish Farmers' Association.

Eight out of 10 Irish cattle are exported and the Irish farming lobby says the mad cow scare has tainted the meat market worldwide and led to traditional customers in the Middle East and elsewhere shunning Irish beef.
Ministers are expected to call for a major expansion of a fund to promote beef consumption both in the EU and world markets to put a floor under falling beef prices.
At present the fund amounts to some 10 million Ecus ($12 million) and EU officials said it could be increased as much as five-fold.
Ministers are also expected to bring forward aid payments to beef farmers from the 1997 budget to the current budget which could make a further 500 million Ecus available in compensation this year.
This would be in addition to some 850 million Ecus made available in emergency aid funds so far since the crisis erupted in March this year.
Officials said the meeting might also agree to buy more surplus beef from the market to stop prices collapsing. The beef is frozen in EU storage for export.

Britain has come in for sharp criticism from its partners for announcing last week that new scientific evidence showed the slaughter of up to 147,000 young cattle agreed in Florence would not speed up the eradication of BSE.
It suspended plans to carry out the cull but is going ahead with the slaughter of up to one million older cattle a year to try to stamp out Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).
